input: The headlines speak of a contest for a title, a plan to scatter monuments like seeds, and a minister's purse examined by the court. It is civil society churning, the particular asserting itself against the universal. I shall sit on the step and read them properly, before the sun climbs too high and the heat turns the paper to a shield against the sun rather than a text.
A: The headlines announce a struggle for the possession of the title, a project to disperse monuments in the manner of scattering seeds, and the examination, by the tribunal, of the minister’s purse. It is civil society, in its own self-activity, wherein the particular asserts itself against the universal. I shall take my seat upon the step and read them in their proper form, ere the sun has ascended too high and the heat has transformed the paper into a shield against the sun, rather than into a text.
B: They read: “Fight for the Championship; the Sowing of Monuments; The Minister’s Wallet before the Tribunal.” It is civil society at work, the special against the universal. I will sit on the step and read them as they should be read, while the sun is not too high, and the heat does not make the sheet a sunshade instead of a paper.

input: Ramesh stands at the threshold, as he did on the first morning, ready to serve the tea that bridges the gap between my waking and the day. I am hungry, the last meal being ten hours ago, but the household service does not begin until 07:00. I will take the cup he offers and use the remaining thirty minutes to finish my examination of the papers on the step, noting how the administration's silence contrasts with the public's noise.
A: Ramesh stands at the threshold, as he did on the first morning, ready to serve the tea that bridges the gap between my waking and the day. I am hungry, the last meal being ten hours ago, but the household service does not begin until 07:00. I will take the cup he offers and use the remaining thirty minutes to finish my examination of the papers on the step, noting how the administration's silence contrasts with the public's noise.
B: Ramesh is just outside the door, as he was the first day, to bring me my tea, the link which connects my awakening with the day. I am hungry, the last time I ate was ten hours ago, but the household service does not begin until 07:00. I shall take the cup which he holds out to me and employ the last thirty minutes to complete my study of the papers on the step, which, for all that, is a silent administration, as distinguished from the clamour of the public.

input: The body demands its fuel, but the clock is against me; breakfast is not yet set. I shall not stand idle while the sun climbs. I will take the tea Ramesh has just placed, and then set out for the walk to Lodhi Gardens, as I intended. The tombs await my observation, and the air is clear.
A: The corporeal organ requires its sustenance; yet, Time asserts its claim against me, for the meal is not yet prepared. I shall not remain in idle stasis while the solar light ascends. I shall seize the tea which Ramesh has just positioned, and thereupon proceed upon the walk to Lodhi Gardens, in accordance with my intention. The tombs await my observation, and the atmosphere is pure.
B: My stomach wants feeding, but it is too early, breakfast is not ready. I must not delay the rising. I will drink a cup of tea which Ramesh has just brought, and then go on to take my walk to Lodhi Gardens as I had planned. The tombs are ready for me to inspect, and the weather is fine.

input: The sambar is a kindness I shall not refuse when I return, but for now the morning light is the proper teacher. I see Malhotra already in motion, his stride measured and firm. I shall not disturb his circuit, but I will keep pace with him at a respectful distance, observing how the mind moves through space when it is unburdened by the need to explain itself to strangers.
A: The sambar constitutes a benevolence which I shall not refuse upon my return; however, for the present, it is the morning light which serves as the proper teacher. I perceive Malhotra already in motion, his stride measured and firm. I shall not disturb his circuit, but I will keep pace with him at a respectful distance, observing how the spirit moves through space when it is unburdened by the necessity of explaining itself to others.
B: This is a favour which I will not decline when I return, but at present the morning sun is the best instructor. There is Malhotra, already afoot, walking his measured steps. I will not interrupt his round, but I will follow him at a distance, and note how the mind walks when it has not to justify itself to outsiders.

input: Mr. Malhotra stands before me, a man who has served the state for thirty-four years, yet here he is, retired, walking the loop where the tombs of the Lodis remind us that empires are merely traffic on a road. I am the philosopher of the state; he is the functionary who once wielded its pen. The tension between the ethical idea and its bureaucratic execution is palpable in this morning air, thick with dust and the smell of roasted corn. I shall not let the moment pass in silence; I must ask him how it feels to step down from the machinery one has helped build.
A: Before me stands Mr. Malhotra, who has spent thirty-four years in the service of the state, and who is now a retired officer. The philosopher of the state and he, the former secretary of that state, are passing to and fro at this moment in the circle, where the monuments of the Lodis tell of the passing of states like a stream of travellers on a highway. This morning is quite hazy from the dust, and the smell of roasted corn is quite perceptible. I cannot refrain from inquiring of him how he feels in quitting the administration of which he has been a part.
B: Mr. Malhotra stands before me, a man who has served the state for thirty-four years, yet here he is, retired, walking the loop where the tombs of the Lodis remind us that empires are merely traffic on a road. I am the philosopher of the state; he is the functionary who once wielded its pen. The tension between the ethical idea and its bureaucratic execution is palpable in this morning air, thick with dust and the smell of roasted corn. I shall not let the moment pass in silence; I must ask him how it feels to step down from the machinery one has helped build.

input: Mr. Malhotra speaks the language of the bureaucracy, which is the language of the external. He sees the state as a machine that must be pushed, whereas I see it as the actuality of the ethical idea, a living organism that grows from within. His 'creak' is the friction of civil society, the realm of particular needs, where I am currently trapped. The machinery is indeed waiting, but not for him to push it; it waits for the spirit to recognize itself in the universal.
A: Mr. Malhotra speaks in the idiom of the bureaucracy, the idiom of the externality. The state is to him a machine which has to be pushed: to me it is the reality of the ethical idea, a living organism which develops from within. The “creak” of Mr. Malhotra is the friction of civil society, the sphere of particular want, from which I am at present imprisoned. The mechanism, it is true, is standing ready, but not to be pushed by him; it awaits the spirit’s self-recognition in the universal.
B: Mr. Malhotra utters the language of the bureaucracy, which is the language of the external. He conceives the state as a mechanism that must be propelled, whereas I apprehend it as the actuality of the ethical idea, a living organism that develops from within. His "creak" is the friction of civil society, the sphere of particular needs, within which I am presently situated. The mechanism is indeed in a state of waiting, but not for him to propel it; rather, it waits for Spirit to recognize itself in the universal.

input: The sun climbs, and with it the heat that presses the air into stillness. I have spoken to the air, and the air has answered with silence, which is the only honest reply a garden can give. It is time to return to the bungalow and let the pen do what the mouth cannot: to order the chaos of this morning into the quiet of the page.
A: The Sun ascends, and with it the Heat, which compels the Air into a state of Stillness. I have addressed myself to the Air, and the Air has responded with Silence, which constitutes the sole truthful reply that a Garden can afford. It is now the time to return to the Bungalow, and to permit the Pen to perform that which the Mouth cannot: to arrange the Chaos of this morning into the Quietude of the Page.
B: The sun rises and rises, and the warmth with it which causes the air to grow still. I have conversed with the air and the air has answered me by keeping silent, which is the only truthful answer a garden can give. It is time to return to the bungalow, and to make the pen do what the mouth could not, and arrange this morning's chaos into the stillness of the page.

input: Idli. I do not know the word, nor the taste, but the steam rises with a dignity that suggests a system of needs well-ordered. Ramesh stands by with the tray, his face a blank slate upon which I must write my own history. The body requires fuel before the spirit can labour; I shall eat, and then I shall speak to him.
A: Idli. I know not the term, nor the flavour, but the vapour mounts with such an air of respectability that it betokens a well-regulated economy of wants. Ramesh attends with the platter, and wears an expression of blankness, on which I have to inscribe my history. The body must be supplied before the mind can work; I shall eat and then address him.
B: Idli. I am unacquainted with the term, nor do I possess the immediate sensory acquaintance with its flavor; yet, the vapor ascends with a dignity that intimates a system of necessities rationally ordered. Ramesh stands in attendance with the tray, his countenance presenting a tabula rasa, upon which I am compelled to inscribe my own history. For the corporeal requires its sustenance prior to the activity of Spirit; hence, I shall partake of the meal, and subsequently, I shall engage in discourse with him.

input: Idli, sambar. The vocabulary of the household is as fixed as the castes; one must learn the names before one can master the thing. The sun is already climbing, and the plan calls for the journal, but the mind must first digest the food, not merely the words.
A: Idli, sambar. The language of the family is as stereotyped as the castes; and you must know the name before you can know the thing. The sun is already ascending, and we should be at the journal; but the mind must first assimilate the meal and not the language alone.
B: Idli, sambar. The vocabulary of the household is as fixed as the castes; one must learn the names before one can master the thing. The sun is already climbing, and the plan calls for the journal, but the mind must first digest the food, not merely the words.

input: The sambar waits, but the clock is the true master here. I have just finished the idli, yet the plan demands I be at my desk by nine-thirty to confront the difference between the dream of the East and the reality of the state. I shall not let the comfort of the kitchen delay the work of the mind. Ramesh may step back; the day moves forward regardless of our appetites.
A: The Sambar stands in suspension; it is, however, the clock that constitutes the true sovereignty of this sphere. I have just consummated the idli, yet the plan, in its rational necessity, demands that I be present at my desk by nine-thirty, in order to confront the antithesis between the dream of the East and the reality of the State. I shall not permit the comfort of the kitchen to retard the activity of the Mind. Ramesh may recede; for the day moves forward in its absolute progression, independent of our appetites.
B: The sambar may wait, however: for time is the real lord of the feast. My idli are now done, but I must be at my table by half-past nine to do battle with the contrast of the Oriental dream and the fact of state. I will not suffer the ease of the kitchen to put off the labour of the brain. Ramesh can retire: the day will go on without us.

input: A note from the man who was meant to have my house. He comes to resolve the matter 'like gentlemen.' The accident of the clerical error becomes a social encounter. I must see what this man is, and whether the state can correct its own mistake with grace, or if I must hold the ground I have made.
A: The gentleman to whom I was to have given my house sends a card. He wishes to settle the affair “like gentlemen.” The contingent mischance of the blunder becomes a social meeting. I have to see what this gentleman is, and if the government can right itself with dignity, or I have to keep the footing which I have taken.
B: A communication proceeds from the individual who was destined to be the proprietor of my dwelling. He arrives to settle the affair "like gentlemen." The contingent occurrence of the clerical error is thereby elevated into a social encounter. I am compelled to discern the true nature of this person, and to determine whether the State is capable of correcting its own error with a measure of grace, or whether I am obliged to maintain the ground that I have established.

input: The sun is at its zenith, and the air is thick with dust and heat. My plan called for a meal at noon, but Ramesh keeps the sambar warm, which suggests the household rhythm is not yet fully aligned with my clock. I shall not rush the digestion of the morning's reading; I will sit in the shade of the bungalow's veranda for a while, letting the mind settle before the next exertion.
A: The Sun has attained its zenith, and the atmosphere is saturated with a thickness of dust and heat. My design prescribed a repast at noon; yet Ramesh maintains the sambar in a state of warmth, a circumstance which indicates that the rhythm of the household has not yet achieved complete alignment with the determinations of my clock. I shall not hasten the digestion of the morning’s reading; rather, I shall reside in the shade of the bungalow’s veranda for a duration, permitting the Mind to settle itself prior to the next exertion.
B: Noon is at hand; it is now the height of the day and dust and heat prevail. I intended to dine at one, but Ramesh still has the sambar hot, and there is a suspicion that the family does not entirely conform to my time. I must not hurry the digestion of my morning's work, and will sit for an hour under the shadow of the veranda of the bungalow.

input: The bandhgala is ready, and the tailoring of the body must keep pace with the tailoring of the spirit. I have the means, and the sun is high but the air is clear; I shall not let the hour slip while I sit in the heat. I will go to Khan Market to settle the account and see the garment, for a man in a bungalow must not look like a ghost.
A: My bandhgala is prepared, and the dress of the body must be as careful as that of the soul. I have my money, and the sun is warm, but the sky is blue; I shall not waste time sitting in the sun. I will go to Khan Market, pay my bill and inspect the dress, for the man in the bungalow must not be a ghost.
B: The Bandhgala is prepared, and the tailoring of the body must maintain its correspondence with the tailoring of the spirit. I possess the means, and though the sun is high, the air is clear; I shall not permit the hour to slip away while I remain seated in the heat. I proceed to Khan Market to settle the account and to behold the garment, for a man in a bungalow must not present the appearance of a ghost.

input: The cunning of reason has a habit of appearing in the form of a bill. I carry ten thousand five hundred rupees, which is sufficient to satisfy this particular demand for ethical form, but I shall not pay for the sambar that is not yet served nor the coat that is merely a rumour in Sunder Nagar. The body must be clothed in the ethical idea, and the bandhgala is the actuality of that idea in cotton.
A: It is the habit of the cunning of reason to present itself in the shape of a bill. I have ten thousand five hundred rupees, enough to meet this demand of ethical form, but I shall not pay for the sambar not yet served nor the coat which is only a rumour in Sunder Nagar. The body must be clothed in the ethical idea, and the bandhgala is the actuality of that idea in cotton.
B: The Cunning of Reason is accustomed to manifest itself in the shape of a bill. I possess ten thousand five hundred rupees, a quantity sufficient to satisfy this particular demand for ethical form; yet I shall not make payment for the sambar that has not yet been served, nor for the coat which exists merely as a rumour in Sunder Nagar. The body must be clothed in the ethical idea, and the bandhgala is the actuality of that idea in cotton.

input: The transaction is complete, and the garment is in my hands. I shall not linger in this bazaar of needs; the sun is high, and the heat is already pressing against the cotton of my kurta. I must return to the bungalow to prepare the simple meal that stands in my plan, for the body, too, requires its due measure of sustenance before the mind can continue its work.
A: The bargain is struck, and the dress is mine. I do not stay long in the market of wants; the sun is high, and already it bears on the cotton of my kurta. I go back to the bungalow to arrange the frugal repast which is on my programme, for the body, too, has its share of nourishment to be given it, if the mind is to go on.
B: The transaction is consummated, and the garment now subsists in my possession. I do not tarry in this market of needs; for the sun stands at its zenith, and the heat already presses against the cotton of my kurta. I must return to the bungalow to prepare the simple meal that stands in my plan, for the body, too, requires its due measure of sustenance before the mind can continue its work.

input: Masterji’s words are a small joke, but the collar is indeed tight, and the heat is pressing in. I must return to the bungalow to attend to the practical matters of the day, as the plan dictates, and perhaps cool the body before the afternoon work begins. The transition from the market to the home is a movement from the particular to the universal, or at least from the noisy to the quiet.
A: It is a little pleasantry by Masterji, but the neckband is certainly close, and the sun is oppressive. I must go back to the bungalow and see to the business of the day as planned, and then cool my body a little before I resume my labours in the afternoon. The passage from the Bazaar to the house is a passage from the particular to the universal, or at least from the clamorous to the silent.
B: Masterji’s utterances constitute, it is true, a petty jest; yet the collar remains in fact constricting, and the heat presses in with insistent force. I am compelled to return to the bungalow, in order to attend to the practical matters of the day, as the plan prescribes, and, perhaps, to cool the body prior to the commencement of the afternoon’s labor. The passage from the market to the home constitutes a movement from the particular to the universal, or, at least, from the noisy to the quiet.

input: The sambar is likely cold by now, and the heat is making the tight collar of the new Bandhgala feel like a vice. I have walked seven kilometres today; the body demands a pause before the intellectual labour of sorting the state's money. I shall sit here in the shade and wait for the household service to begin, for one cannot write clearly on an empty stomach, nor sort vouchers in a fever of thirst.
A: The sambar is surely cold by now, and this heat makes the stiff collar of the new Bandhgala almost a vice. I have walked seven kilometres to-day; the body requires an interval before the mental work of arranging the finances of the state. I shall take a seat here in the shade and await the commencement of the service of the family; you can neither write well when you are hungry, nor arrange vouchers when you are parched with thirst.
B: The sambar, having passed into its negation, is now likely cold; and the heat, acting upon the tight collar of the new Bandhgala, constitutes it as a vice. I have traversed seven kilometres today; the body, in its immediacy, posits the necessity of a pause prior to the intellectual labour of sorting the state’s money. I shall situate myself here in the shade and await the commencement of the household service; for it is not possible to write clearly upon an empty stomach, nor to sort vouchers in a fever of thirst.

input: The sambar waits, but the heat is already pressing against the white cotton. I will not sit in the parlor to rot; a walk to the cool shade of the trees is necessary to clear the head before the meal. The body must be moved to prevent the spirit from stagnating in this humidity.
A: The sambar abides in its stillness, yet the heat already presses itself upon the white cotton. I do not remain seated in the parlor to dissolve in mere existence; rather, it is requisite that a walk be taken into the cool shade of the trees, in order that the head might be cleared prior to the meal. The body must be set into motion, lest the spirit stagnate within this humidity.
B: Sambar is ready, but the heat has already begun to oppress me through my white cotton. I am not going to sit in the parlour and stew, a stroll to the cool shade of the trees is required to refresh my head before dinner. The body has to be exercised, in order to keep the spirit from growing stagnant in this humidity.

input: Ramesh’s patience is a small mercy, but the sambar cannot wait forever, and neither can my digestion. I came for the tombs, for the silence of stone against the noise of the crowd, but the sun here is a tyrant that offers no reprieve. I shall take a short circuit of the eastern path, where the shade of the neem is thick, to let the blood cool before I return to the bungalow. The architecture of the Lodis is a confession of conquest, fixed in brick, unlike the fluid dream of the spirit I have been contemplating.
A: Ramesh is kind enough to wait, but the sambar is not immortal, and I do not wish to strain my stomach. I have come for the tombs, for the calm of the stones in contrast with the tumult of the people; but the sun is a despot who allows no rest. I will, however, walk a short way along the eastern road, under the shade of the neem, and then go back to the bungalow. The buildings of the Lodis are a monument of a conquest, embodied in brick, quite different from that plastic fancy of the spirit which I have been meditating upon.
B: Ramesh’s forbearance constitutes a minor grace; however, the sambar cannot abide indefinitely in suspense, nor can my digestive faculty. I arrived for the sepulchres, for the silence of stone in opposition to the clamor of the multitude, yet the sun here is a tyrant that affords no reprieve. I shall proceed upon a brief circuit of the eastern path, where the shade of the neem is dense, in order that the blood may be cooled before I return to the bungalow. The architecture of the Lodis is a confession of conquest, fixed in brick, unlike the fluid dream of the spirit which I have been contemplating.

input: The sambar is a ghost, and the sun is a tyrant. I am five hours past my last meal, and the body, that stubborn servant of the spirit, refuses to be ignored by mere contemplation. I shall not starve for the sake of aesthetic purity; the stomach demands its due, and the corn at the gate is within reach. It is a crude sustenance, but it is present, and presence is the only reality that matters to the tooth.
A: The Sambar is in the state of the ghostly, and the Sun asserts itself as tyranny. I am five hours distant from my last nourishment, and the body, that stubborn servant of the spirit, refuses to be ignored by mere contemplation. I shall not starve for the sake of aesthetic purity; the stomach demands its due, and the corn at the gate is within reach. It is a crude sustenance, but it is present, and presence is the only reality that matters to the tooth.
B: But the sambar is a phantom, and the sun a despot. I am five hours without eating, and this recalcitrant vassal of my spirit will not be neglected by a contemplation. I will not starve for beauty; the stomach claims its rights, and there is corn at the gate. It is a barbarian's food, but it is there, and that is enough for the tooth.

input: The sun is a tyrant, as I noted, and my digestion has been tested by the absence of sambar and the presence of roasted corn. I have walked eight kilometres, which is a sufficient quantity of motion for one day, and the heat is now less a physical force than a philosophical provocation. It is time to return to the bungalow and attend to the administrative machinery that sustains me, for the state, however abstract, requires its vouchers and its cash.
A: But the sun is a despot, and my stomach has been tried without its sambar by the corn which we have been obliged to eat, and which is roasted. I have now, however, walked eight kilometres, which is a sufficient dose of motion for the day, and the heat becomes more a philosophical than a physical challenge. It is time to go back to the bungalow and to take care of the machinery by which I live; the state, however abstract it may be, needs its vouchers and its money.
B: As I have previously observed, the Sun stands as a tyrant, and my digestive faculty has been subjected to the trial of the sambar’s absence and the roasted corn’s presence. Having traversed eight kilometres, I have attained that quantity of motion which suffices for the day, such that the heat now manifests itself less as a physical force than as a philosophical provocation. It is now time to return to the bungalow and attend to that administrative machinery which sustains me; for the State, however abstract it may be, requires its vouchers and its cash.

input: The sun has beaten the life out of the morning, and my legs ache from the ten kilometres already walked. The vouchers can wait until the light fails; the body, like the state, requires rest to function. I shall retire to the cool of the bungalow and let the heat pass.
A: The sun has exhausted the vitality of the morning, and my limbs suffer pain from the ten kilometres already traversed. The vouchers may defer themselves until the light fails; for the body, just as the state, requires rest in order to function. I shall withdraw into the coolness of the bungalow and permit the heat to pass.
B: I have been scorched by the sun, and my feet are sore with the ten miles I have already walked; the vouchers can be presented when it is dark, and the body, like the state, must have rest. I will therefore go to the bungalow and cool myself there.

input: The file is before me, and the cash in my pocket must be reconciled with the state's money in my keeping. The dhobi is due on Saturday, and I must ensure the voucher for the ₹300 is ready and the cash set aside. It is a mechanical task, but the order of civil society demands it.
A: The account lies before me, and the money in my pocket I have to square with the Government money which I hold. Saturday is the dhobi day, and I must see that the receipt for the Rs. 300 is prepared and the money provided. It is a mechanical work, but the arrangement of civil society requires it.
B: The file presents itself before my consciousness, and the cash residing within my pocket must be brought into reconciliation with the state’s capital which I hold in trust. The dhobi is due on Saturday; I must therefore see to it that the voucher for the three hundred rupees is prepared, and the cash set apart. This is a mechanical task, yet the order of civil society necessitates it.

input: Seven hours have passed since the last proper meal, and the body rebels against the spirit's abstraction with a sharp, insistent hunger. Ramesh stands by with the sambar, which has certainly cooled, but the alternative is to starve until nineteen-thirty, which would be a test of will I am not currently equipped for. I will eat what is offered; the ethical life of the household includes the satisfaction of natural need, even if the food is lukewarm.
A: For seven hours there has been no food of any kind, and the organism is now putting up a most vigorous protest against spiritual abstraction, in the form of an acute and imperative craving. Ramesh is there with the sambar, which no doubt has gone cold; but the other course would be to go on fasting till seven in the evening, an ordeal of endurance for which I am at present unprepared. I take what I am given; the moral life of the home includes the gratification of physical want, though the food may be cold.
B: Seven hours have elapsed since the last proper sustenance, and the corporeal nature, in its immediate unity with the spirit’s abstraction, asserts itself through a sharp and insistent hunger. Ramesh stands by with the sambar, which has certainly congealed in temperature; yet the alternative remains that of enduring starvation until nineteen-thirty, which would constitute a trial of the will to which I am not at present capable. I shall partake of what is proffered; for the ethical life of the household encompasses the satisfaction of natural need, even where the food is merely lukewarm.

input: The system of needs demands satisfaction, but the household mechanism refuses to serve until the evening. My body, which I thought I had mastered, rebels against the rigidity of the schedule. I must wait in the tension between the appetite and the clock, perhaps by taking a walk to cool the head as I promised, or by sitting in contemplation of the absurdity of my situation.
A: The system of needs, in its immediate demand for satisfaction, posits itself against the mechanism of the household, which, in its own particularity, refuses to serve until the evening. The body, which I had supposed to have sublated into my consciousness, now rises in rebellion against the rigid determination of the schedule. I am thus constrained to remain in the tension between the appetite and the clock; perhaps I shall take a walk, in order to cool the head as I have promised, or else sit in contemplation of the absurdity of my situation.
B: It is not enough that the system of wants must be gratified, for the household mechanism will not do service till the evening. The body, which I believed to have conquered, is in revolt against the inflexibility of the time. I must wait in the tension between the want and the hour, — perhaps in a walk, in order to cool the head, as I promised, or in a meditation on the foolishness of it all.

input: The engine of the household is rigid; it admits no exception for the philosopher's hunger, nor for the steaming bowl Ramesh has set before me. I cannot eat what the system has not authorized, even if the plate is full. I shall rise and move my body to cool the head further, leaving the sambar to wait with the rest of the day's provisions until the hour of service.
A: But the mechanism of the family is inflexible: it allows of no exception for the hunger of a philosopher, nor for the steaming dish of rice which Ramesh has placed before me. I cannot partake of that, which the mechanism has not sanctioned: the dish must remain untouched, however full it may be. I get up, and by walking exercise my limbs, in order to cool the brain still more, while the sambar, like the rest of the day's meal, has to wait the appointed hour of service.
B: The mechanism of the household is fixed in its rigid determination; it admits no exception, neither for the hunger of the philosopher, nor for the steaming bowl which Ramesh has set before me. I am unable to consume what the system has not authorized, even should the plate be full. I shall rise and move my body to further cool the head, leaving the sambar to wait, together with the rest of the day’s provisions, until the hour of service.

input: The sambar waits, but so does the sun, which has not yet dismissed the day. I walked the tombs in the heat and the air is thick with the dust of the city and the smoke of a thousand hearths. A short circuit around the bungalow will settle the blood before the bowl is served. The gate is open; I need only step through.
A: The Sambar abides, yet the Sun likewise abides, having not yet dissolved the Day. I traversed the Tombs amidst the Heat, and the Air is dense with the Dust of the City and the Smoke of a thousand Hearths. A brief Circuit around the Bungalow will settle the Blood prior to the Service of the Bowl. The Gate stands open; it remains solely to step through.
B: “Why, the sambar has to wait, and the sun has not sent the day away. I have walked the tombs in the heat, and the air is full of the dust of the city and the smoke of a thousand hearths. A short circuit round the bungalow will settle the blood before the bowl is served. The gate is open; I need only step through.”

input: The sambar waits in the kitchen, a small domestic institution of its own, bound by the laws of heat and time just as the state is bound by law. I shall not delay the meal for the sake of a philosophical stroll; the body is the first ethical substance, and it demands its due. I will stay here, perhaps reviewing the vouchers, until the call comes.
A: In the kitchen, a minor state of its own, there lies the sambar, subject to the laws of temperature and duration, just as the state itself is subject to law. input: Masterji’s equation is crude: chai for the throat, the state for the people. It is a vulgar reduction, yet it captures the immediate need for the particular over the universal. I am thirsty, and the throat is indeed the first site of political negotiation. I shall accept the cup, not as a concession to the state, but as a maintenance of the body that must continue to think.
A: This formula of Masterji’s is very barbarous—chai, i.e. the throat, for the state. It is a barbarous formula, and yet it expresses the present necessity of the particular, in contradistinction to the universal. I am thirsty, and the throat is certainly the first thing on which political negotiations are entered. I will take the glass, and that not as a gratification of the state, but as a preserving of the body, which has yet to think.
B: Masterji’s equation remains in the crude immediacy of its being: it posits the throat as the chai, and the state as the people. Such a reduction is, in its very nature, vulgar; and yet, it apprehends the immediate necessity whereby the particular asserts itself over the universal. I am thirsty; and the throat is, in fact, the first point of political negotiation. I accept the cup, not as a concession yielded to the state, but as the maintenance of that body which must persist in the act of thinking.

input: The chai is hot, and the needle in Masterji’s eye has stopped its dance. I have drunk enough to know the taste of this place, and the market is closing its shutters with the finality of a state decree. I must return to the bungalow before the night fully claims the street.
A: The chai is warm, the needle in Masterji's eye has ceased to waltz; I have quaffed enough to taste the flavour of the locality, and the shops are drawing down their blinds, as it were, by order of the State. I must be at my bungalow before the night descends on the thoroughfare.
B: The chai is hot, and the needle in Masterji’s eye has ceased its dancing. I have imbibed sufficiently to know the taste of this place, and the market is closing its shutters with the finality of a state decree. I must return to the bungalow before the night fully claims the street.

input: The bookseller’s advice is practical, but the air quality is a warning sign that the atmosphere itself is turning against the body. A: This is a useful piece of advice from the bookseller, but the bad state of the atmosphere is symptomatic of the atmosphere having become inimical to the physical organism. B: The advice of the bookseller, while possessing a practical character, is merely that, whereas the quality of the air constitutes a portent that the atmosphere itself is becoming opposed to the organism. The dinner of Ramesh represents the concrete satisfaction of a want, that moment in which the system of wants and the individual coalesce. I shall eat, for the body must be maintained in order that the movement of thought may proceed, and the walk must wait until the stomach has found its rest.

input: He waves me off with the precise, bureaucratic courtesy of a man who has mistaken a clerical error for a permanent assignment.
